understand.concept: Python offers different rounding operations with different rules. The built-in round() rounds to a requested number of decimal places and uses ties-to-even for exact halfway cases. math.ceil() returns the smallest integer not less than a value, math.floor() returns the greatest integer not greater than it, and math.trunc() removes the fractional part toward zero.
understand.whyItMatters: Choosing the correct rounding rule matters in measurements, pagination, allocation and reporting. Similar-looking functions can produce different results for negative values.
understand.analogy: Imagine a lift moving between floors: ceiling always moves to the next floor above, floor moves to the floor below, while truncation moves toward zero.
understand.analogyLimit: Rounding binary floating-point values can expose representation effects; decimal currency calculations may require decimal.Decimal and an explicit rounding policy.
understand.summary: Rounding Numbers with ceil(), floor() and trunc() teaches practical use of math.ceil(), math.floor(), math.trunc(), round() with correct input and precision handling.

explain.narrative:
## Four distinct operations
`round(value, ndigits)` rounds to a number of decimal places; ties are rounded to the nearest even result. `math.ceil(x)` and `math.floor(x)` return integers around the value. `math.trunc(x)` discards the fractional part toward zero.

For positive numbers these operations may look similar, but negative inputs reveal the distinction: floor moves toward negative infinity, while truncation moves toward zero. Use a rule that matches the domain requirement and document it.

examples.explanation: ceil returns the smallest integer greater than or equal to the input.

examples.title: Round downward
examples.explanation: floor moves toward negative infinity, including for negative values.

examples.title: Truncate toward zero
examples.explanation: trunc removes the fractional part without rounding away from zero.

examples.title: Compare all three integer operations
examples.code:
import math
value = -2.7
print(math.ceil(value), math.floor(value), math.trunc(value))
examples.explanation: The negative input makes the difference between floor and truncation visible.
